title: When the Measure Becomes the Goal
objective: After this level you can explain Goodhart's law: why a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it.
summary: Goodhart's law: a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it. Goodhart said it in 1975; Strathern's 1997 wording made it famous.

cards.headline: Imagine a reading contest: one sticker per book. Watch the thin books vanish.
cards.body: Nobody cheats, exactly. The children simply do what the contest rewards. The count of books shoots up, but it stops telling you how much anyone is reading. There's a law for this, and it started in economics.

cards.headline: Goodhart's law
cards.body: In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart was writing about monetary policy, where officials steered by targets for growth in the money supply. He put the problem this way: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." In plain words: a number that tracks something well can stop tracking it once people push on it.

cards.headline: The famous wording isn't his
cards.body: The version most people quote came later. In a 1997 paper on audits in British universities, the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern summed it up: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." What began as a jocular aside became a widely applied idea, far beyond economics.

cards.headline: Why the number breaks
cards.body: A measure is only a sign of what you want. Reward the sign, and people find cheaper ways to produce it. Judge scholars by how many papers they publish, and you encourage "salami slicing": dividing the findings of one study into many separate papers. Quantity wins over quality. The count rises; the science doesn't. People respond to incentives.

cards.headline: Goodhart's law: learned
learned: Reward a sign and people fake the sign

questions.prompt: Whose wording is "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"?

options.label: Charles Goodhart's, in 1975
options.rationale: Goodhart's own wording was about statistical regularities collapsing.

options.label: John Stuart Mill's, in 1843
options.rationale: Mill wrote about causes as the sum of conditions.

options.label: David Hume's, in 1748
options.rationale: Hume defined cause; he didn't write about targets.

questions.explanation: Goodhart stated the idea in 1975; the famous wording is the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's, from 1997.

questions.prompt: Why does judging scholars by their number of papers backfire?

options.label: Papers are too expensive to publish
options.rationale: Cost isn't the problem Goodhart's law describes.

options.label: People split one study into many papers
Journals stop accepting new papers
options.rationale: Nothing like that happens in the example.

options.label: Scholars refuse to write any papers
options.rationale: The opposite: the count goes up.

questions.explanation: Rewarding the count encourages salami slicing: the number rises without more or better research.

questions.prompt: "Our paper count doubled, so our research improved." Which unstated premise does Goodhart's law question?

options.label: Doubling a number is always good news
options.rationale: Too broad, and not what the argument relies on.

options.label: Research should be published quickly
options.rationale: A value judgment the argument doesn't need.

options.label: More researchers joined the team
options.rationale: Not needed: the argument is about the count reflecting quality.

options.label: The count still tracks research quality

questions.explanation: The argument assumes the count still reflects quality. Once the count is a target, that hidden premise may fail.
